outcomes.question: We lodged our annual return on 19 October 2026. Was the new question about a person carrying out the chief executive officer role already mandatory for that filing?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ACRA annual return officer particulars and CEO role confirmation** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** From 20 October 2026, an annual-return filer must confirm that current particulars already provided to ACRA are accurate for directors, chief executive officers (CEOs), secretaries, auditors and relevant members. These particulars include names, identification details, nationality, contact address, appointment dates, registered office address and shareholding details where applicable. The form separately asks whether any individual performs the CEO role. A company limited by guarantee must confirm its latest-reported total member count. Applies to annual returns filed from the expressly stated commencement date. Check ACRA-recorded particulars and update inaccurate particulars in Bizfile before filing. The CEO question concerns individuals performing the role; the ACRA notice does not limit it to a title or appointed position. Companies limited by guarantee have an additional total-number-of-members confirmation. The notice does not say the CEO question or officer-particulars confirmation changes the underlying duty to appoint or register officers. A case-specific conclusion requires: For a particular filing: filing date, company type, existing ACRA particulars, whether individuals perform the CEO role, and whether the company is limited by guarantee. General change explanation only; does not verify what particulars are currently recorded for an entity. Do not apply this change to filings submitted before 20 October 2026 without contemporaneous evidence. The notice gives examples of particulars and says “where applicable”; it is not a field-by-field eform schema. The stated commencement does not make this new change applicable to the filing date supplied before 20 October 2026. This notice does not establish the complete requirements that governed that earlier filing. [ACRA | Commencement of Key Changes under the Corporate and Accounting Laws (Amendment) Act 2025 on 20 October 2026](https://www.acra.gov.sg/news-events/news-announcements/commencement-of-key-changes-under-the-corporate-and-accounting-laws--amendment--act-2025-on-20-october-2026/)

outcomes.question: For ACRA financial-statement filing, is meeting the small-company size limits enough to use Simplified XBRL if the company is publicly accountable?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ACRA XBRL financial statement filing requirements and exemptions** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** The ACRA guidance lists simplified XBRL plus an authorised PDF for smaller and non-publicly accountable companies; XBRL FSH (Banks) or XBRL FSH (Insurance) plus an authorised PDF for the regulated bank, finance and insurance group; PDF only for companies limited by guarantee or companies approved to use other standards; and Full XBRL for all other Singapore-incorporated companies required to file financial statements. “Smaller” requires both current-year revenue and assets not exceeding S$500,000. “Non-publicly accountable” also excludes listed and specified regulated entity types. The dormant-relevant-company and solvent-EPC financial-statement exceptions have separate qualification conditions. ACRA labels technical resources as applying from 19 October 2026 onwards and identifies ACRA Taxonomy 2026 resources. A company must first determine whether it is required to file financial statements; dormant relevant companies and solvent EPCs may qualify for separate financial-statement exceptions. Small-company revenue and asset thresholds must both be met; group consolidation and currency translation details apply under the ACRA definitions page. The Full/Simplified/FSH/PDF template depends on the company’s exact status and regulatory category. Dormant relevant companies need not prepare/file only if all Companies Act section 201A requirements are met, including the assets, dormancy and listing/subsidiary conditions. A solvent EPC meeting an EPC definition may elect not to file financial statements but may file voluntarily; its annual-return solvency declaration still applies. Foreign companies with Singapore branches and some individually approved cases are addressed elsewhere on the ACRA filing guidance and are not classified by this local-company rule summary. A case-specific conclusion requires: Local/foreign incorporation, company form and whether it is a company limited by guarantee. Required-to-file/exempt status, dormancy history, listed/subsidiary status and group assets. Current-year revenue and assets, consolidation and currency facts. Public-accountability or MAS regulatory status. EPC status and solvency, where relevant. Does not determine an individual company’s template without classification facts. The complete definitions and section 201A eligibility must be checked against ACRA’s linked guidance and law. Do not apply the current page or 19 October 2026 XBRL boundary to a historical filing unless the relevant year-specific official source supports it. [ACRA | Financial statements: Filing requirements and exemptions](https://www.acra.gov.sg/manage/companies/legal-requirements-common-offences/filing-financial-statements-in-xbrl-format/requirements-exemptions/)

#### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Withholding tax filing and payment deadline** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS requires WHT filing and payment by the 15th of the second month after its defined date of payment. For most payments, use the earliest of the contractual due date (or invoice date if there is no agreement, ignoring credit terms), credit to an account designated by the non-resident, and actual payment. Director fees have separate timing rules based on arrears/advance approval, entitlement, credit and actual payment. WHT still must be filed when a DTA or ARI makes the rate zero. GIRO is normally deducted on the 25th of the due month, or the next working day if that date is a weekend/public holiday. The exact deadline requires the payment type and all relevant dates. Withholding Tax (WHT) Filing and Payment Due Date

Payers must file and pay the WHT to IRAS by the due date.

WHT must be filed even if the payment to a non-resident is exempted under the Avoidance of Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) or Approved Royalties Incentive (ARI).

On this page:

As a payer, you must file and pay WHT to IRAS by the 15th of the second month from the date of payment to the non-resident.

Learn more through our e-Learning video on the Filing and Payment of WHT.

If you are on GIRO for WHT payment, the GIRO deduction date is on the 25th of the month the tax is due. If the GIRO deduction date falls on a weekend or public holiday, the deduction will be made on the next working day.

Refer to your acknowledgement page for payment details after filing WHT.

Definition of date of payment

The date of payment is defined as the earliest of the following dates:

For all payments except director’s fees

• When the payment is due and payable based on the agreement or contract, or the date of the invoice in the absence of any agreement or contract (credit terms should not be taken into consideration).

• When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident

• The date of actual payment

For director’s fees

• When the payment is due and payable under the following scenarios:

◦ Director's fees approved in arrears

For director's fees approved in arrears, the director has already rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned. However, the director's fees must be disclosed to and approved by members of the company before they can be paid to him. Hence, the earliest date on which the director is entitled to the director's fees, is the date the fees are voted and approved at the company's AGM.

◦ Director's fees approved in advance

For director's fees approved in advance, the director may not have rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned when the fees are approved at the company's AGM. Hence, the earliest date on which the director can be entitled to the director's fees, is as and when he renders his services.

•

• When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident

• The date of actual payment

Scenarios | Date of payment to the non-resident  

Filing and payment due date

Technical assistance fees
A non-resident company issued an invoice dated 26 Mar 2025 to a payer for technical assistance fees in respect of services rendered. The invoice stated that the amount must be paid within 30 days.
The payer received the invoice on 30 Apr 2025 and paid the non-resident on 19 May 2025.  | 26 Mar 2025
(based on invoice date)  | 15 May 2025

For GIRO payer, deduction takes place on 26 May 2025.

Royalty payment
The agreement stated that royalties at 5% of sales shall accrue to the non-resident at the end of each quarter.
In this instance, the royalty period from Apr to Jun 2025 was accrued on 30 Jun 2025 (end of quarter), and the royalty payment was made to the non-resident on 15 Jul 2025. | 30 Jun 2025
(based on date of accrual)  | 15 Aug 2025

For GIRO payer, deduction takes place on 25 Aug 2025.

Director’s fee
The director’s fee of $50,000 for the period from 01 Jan 2024 to 31 Dec 2024, was voted and approved in the company's Annual General Meeting (AGM) on 2 Jul 2025.
However, the fee was only paid to the director on 29 Sep 2025.  | 2 Jul 2025
(based on AGM date)  | 15 Sep 2025

For GIRO payer, deduction takes place on 25 Sep 2025.

Multiple payments for a single engagement (non-resident professional or public entertainer)

If you have made multiple payments to the same non-resident professional or non-resident public entertainer for the same engagement within a 60-day period, you can consolidate the various payments into 1 filing and declare the last payment date as the date of payment to the non-resident professional or public entertainer.

Late payment penalty

Penalties will be imposed if the WHT is paid to IRAS after the payment due date or if the GIRO deduction is unsuccessful.

FAQs

Can I consolidate and file my WHT submission?

Yes, you can consolidate and file WHT twice a year, on 15 June and 15 December of each year if you are claiming tax exemption (i.e. tax rate is 0%) under the DTA and ARI.

For example:

Your WHT exempted (i.e. tax rate is 0%) payment to a non-resident is due every 15 of the month. Instead of filing for WHT monthly, you can consolidate and file 6 records on 15 June and the remaining 6 records on 15 December.

Payers must file and pay the WHT to IRAS by the due date.

WHT must be filed even if the payment to a non-resident is exempted under the Avoidance of Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) or Approved Royalties Incentive (ARI).

On this page:

As a payer, you must file and pay WHT to IRAS by the 15th of the second month from the date of payment to the non-resident.

Learn more through our e-Learning video on the Filing and Payment of WHT.

If you are on GIRO for WHT payment, the GIRO deduction date is on the 25th of the month the tax is due. If the GIRO deduction date falls on a weekend or public holiday, the deduction will be made on the next working day.

Refer to your acknowledgement page for payment details after filing WHT.

Definition of date of payment

The date of payment is defined as the earliest of the following dates:

For all payments except director’s fees

• When the payment is due and payable based on the agreement or contract, or the date of the invoice in the absence of any agreement or contract (credit terms should not be taken into consideration).

• When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident

• The date of actual payment

For director’s fees

• When the payment is due and payable under the following scenarios:

◦ Director's fees approved in arrears

For director's fees approved in arrears, the director has already rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned. However, the director's fees must be disclosed to and approved by members of the company before they can be paid to him. Hence, the earliest date on which the director is entitled to the director's fees, is the date the fees are voted and approved at the company's AGM.

◦ Director's fees approved in advance

For director's fees approved in advance, the director may not have rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned when the fees are approved at the company's AGM. Hence, the earliest date on which the director can be entitled to the director's fees, is as and when he renders his services.

• When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident

• The date of actual payment

Filing and payment due date

Technical assistance fees
A non-resident company issued an invoice dated 26 Mar 2025 to a payer for technical assistance fees in respect of services rendered. The invoice stated that the amount must be paid within 30 days.
The payer received the invoice on 30 Apr 2025 and paid the non-resident on 19 May 2025.  | 26 Mar 2025
(based on invoice date)  | 15 May 2025

For GIRO payer, deduction takes place on 26 May 2025.

Royalty payment
The agreement stated that royalties at 5% of sales shall accrue to the non-resident at the end of each quarter.
In this instance, the royalty period from Apr to Jun 2025 was accrued on 30 Jun 2025 (end of quarter), and the royalty payment was made to the non-resident on 15 Jul 2025. | 30 Jun 2025
(based on date of accrual)  | 15 Aug 2025

For GIRO payer, deduction takes place on 25 Aug 2025.

Director’s fee
The director’s fee of $50,000 for the period from 01 Jan 2024 to 31 Dec 2024, was voted and approved in the company's Annual General Meeting (AGM) on 2 Jul 2025.
However, the fee was only paid to the director on 29 Sep 2025.  | 2 Jul 2025
(based on AGM date)  | 15 Sep 2025

For GIRO payer, deduction takes place on 25 Sep 2025.

Multiple payments for a single engagement (non-resident professional or public entertainer)

If you have made multiple payments to the same non-resident professional or non-resident public entertainer for the same engagement within a 60-day period, you can consolidate the various payments into 1 filing and declare the last payment date as the date of payment to the non-resident professional or public entertainer.

Late payment penalty

Penalties will be imposed if the WHT is paid to IRAS after the payment due date or if the GIRO deduction is unsuccessful.

FAQs

Can I consolidate and file my WHT submission?

Yes, you can consolidate and file WHT twice a year, on 15 June and 15 December of each year if you are claiming tax exemption (i.e. tax rate is 0%) under the DTA and ARI.

For example:

Your WHT exempted (i.e. tax rate is 0%) payment to a non-resident is due every 15 of the month. Instead of filing for WHT monthly, you can consolidate and file 6 records on 15 June and the remaining 6 records on 15 December.

outcomes.question: Our GST-registered business paid for staff medical examinations needed to renew their work permits. Does having a business reason make the GST deductible as input tax?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for the issues identified below; other issues remain incomplete.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** See the evidence gaps and coverage limitations below.

#### IRAS — GST

**Status:** Evidence verified

**GST input tax on staff medical expenses** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS states that staff medical input tax is generally disallowed under regulation 26 of the GST (General) Regulations. Subject to the ordinary input-tax conditions, the stated exceptions are expenses obligatory under WICA or a qualifying Industrial Relations Act collective agreement; or, for expenses incurred on or after 1 October 2021, treatment connected with a work-related health risk or requirement and required under relevant Singapore written law. For the advisory limb, IRAS specifies treatment related to COVID-19 and required under a written advisory of the Government or a Singapore public authority. IRAS specifically says Primary Care Plan expenses do not meet the described work-related exception. A claim needs the expense date, legal/collective-agreement basis, work-related risk and mandate evidence, GST registration and invoice facts. [IRAS | Conditions for Claiming Input Tax](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/goods-services-tax-(gst)/claiming-gst-(input-tax)/conditions-for-claiming-input-tax)

**Source:** IRAS | Conditions for Claiming Input Tax (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports GST input tax on staff medical expenses): Input tax claims are disallowed under Regulation 26 of the GST (General) Regulations.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports GST input tax on staff medical expenses): However, subject to the conditions for input tax claim, these claims are allowed if: • the medical expenses (e.g. pre-employment and annual health screening expenses) are obligatory under the Work Injury Compensation Act (WICA) or under any collective agreement under the Industrial Relations Act (IRA); or • the medical treatment in respect of expenses incurred on or after 1 Oct 2021 is provided in connection with any health risk or requirement due to the work nature or environment and mandated by written law or advisory.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports GST input tax on staff medical expenses): the medical treatment in respect of expenses incurred on or after 1 Oct 2021 is provided in connection with any health risk or requirement arising on account of the nature of the work required of your staff or his work environment; and ◦ the medical expenses are incurred pursuant to any written law of Singapore concerning the medical treatment or the provision of a medical facility or medical practitioner; or ◦ the medical treatment is related to COVID-19 and the staff undergoes such medical treatment pursuant to any written advisory (including industry circular) issued by, or posted on the website of, the Government or a public authority of Singapore.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports GST input tax on staff medical expenses): No, GST incurred on PCP will not be claimable. Based on the nature of the medical expenses covered under the PCP, the medical treatment is not provided in connection with any health risk or requirement arising on account of the nature of the work required of your staff or his work environment (e.g. employees exposed to radiation in the course of their work are required to undergo prescribed medical examinations by an approved medical practitioner). As such, it does not fall under any of the exceptions above and thus GST incurred on PCP will not be claimable.

- Official source: [IRAS | Conditions for Claiming Input Tax](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/goods-services-tax-(gst)/claiming-gst-(input-tax)/conditions-for-claiming-input-tax)

Input tax claims are disallowed under Regulation 26 of the GST (General) Regulations.

However, subject to the conditions for input tax claim, these claims are allowed if: • the medical expenses (e.g. pre-employment and annual health screening expenses) are obligatory under the Work Injury Compensation Act (WICA) or under any collective agreement under the Industrial Relations Act (IRA); or • the medical treatment in respect of expenses incurred on or after 1 Oct 2021 is provided in connection with any health risk or requirement due to the work nature or environment and mandated by written law or advisory.

the medical treatment in respect of expenses incurred on or after 1 Oct 2021 is provided in connection with any health risk or requirement arising on account of the nature of the work required of your staff or his work environment; and ◦ the medical expenses are incurred pursuant to any written law of Singapore concerning the medical treatment or the provision of a medical facility or medical practitioner; or ◦ the medical treatment is related to COVID-19 and the staff undergoes such medical treatment pursuant to any written advisory (including industry circular) issued by, or posted on the website of, the Government or a public authority of Singapore.

No, GST incurred on PCP will not be claimable. Based on the nature of the medical expenses covered under the PCP, the medical treatment is not provided in connection with any health risk or requirement arising on account of the nature of the work required of your staff or his work environment (e.g. employees exposed to radiation in the course of their work are required to undergo prescribed medical examinations by an approved medical practitioner). As such, it does not fall under any of the exceptions above and thus GST incurred on PCP will not be claimable.

Can I claim the GST charged on medical examinations incurred for the purpose of renewing my employees' work permits? No, the input tax on such examinations is blocked as medical expenses under Regulation 26 of the GST (General) Regulations.

### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

#### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Evidence verified

- **CPF rule explanation:** CPF Board’s 2026 contribution table applies from 1 January 2026 to Singapore Citizens or third-year-onward SPRs in private-sector or non-pensionable public-service employment. Updates on 21 May 2026
To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?
The following table summarises the current contribution rates for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third year and onwards) with monthly wages above $750, across the different age groups.
Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34

Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?

Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34
Above 60 to 65 | 12.5 | 12.5 | 25
Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

Updates on 21 May 2026
To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?
The following table summarises the current contribution rates for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third year and onwards) with monthly wages above $750, across the different age groups.
Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34
Above 60 to 65 | 12.5 | 12.5 | 25
Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.

Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status

Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

As a Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR), you are required to make CPF contributions on wages earned in Singapore.
CPF contributions are not payable for employees who are neither Singapore Citizens nor SPRs.
Your CPF contribution rates as an SPR depend on how long you have held Permanent Resident status.
First-year rate: Applies from the day you obtain your SPR status, [i.e. the date indicated on your Entry Permit (Form 5/5A) issued by the Immigration & Checkpoints Authority (ICA)] until the last day of the month of your first anniversary of SPR.
Second-year rate: Applies from the month following your first anniversary as an SPR until the last day of the month of your second anniversary.
Third-year rate: Applies from the month following your second anniversary as an SPR onwards.
Example
If you have obtained your SPR status on 15 January 2026, the start and end dates for first, second and third year of obtaining SPR status are shown in the table below:
Year of obtaining SPR status | Starts from | Ends on
First year | 15 January 2026 | 31 January 2027
Second year | 1 February 2027 | 31 January 2028
Third year | 1 February 2028 | Not applicable

As a Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR), you are required to make CPF contributions on wages earned in Singapore.
CPF contributions are not payable for employees who are neither Singapore Citizens nor SPRs.
Your CPF contribution rates as an SPR depend on how long you have held Permanent Resident status.
First-year rate: Applies from the day you obtain your SPR status, [i.e. the date indicated on your Entry Permit (Form 5/5A) issued by the Immigration & Checkpoints Authority (ICA)] until the last day of the month of your first anniversary of SPR.
Second-year rate: Applies from the month following your first anniversary as an SPR until the last day of the month of your second anniversary.
Third-year rate: Applies from the month following your second anniversary as an SPR onwards.
Example
If you have obtained your SPR status on 15 January 2026, the start and end dates for first, second and third year of obtaining SPR status are shown in the table below:
Year of obtaining SPR status | Starts from | Ends on
First year | 15 January 2026 | 31 January 2027
Second year | 1 February 2027 | 31 January 2028
Third year | 1 February 2028 | Not applicable

### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.

#### Ministry of Manpower — Employment requirements

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Final salary payment deadlines by termination reason** (party in scope: Employee)
- **MOM rule explanation:** For employees covered by the Employment Act, final salary is due on the last employment day when required notice is served; within 7 days of the last employment day when the employee resigns without notice; and, after misconduct dismissal or employer termination, on the last day or, if that is not possible, within 3 working days from dismissal or termination. Commission timing follows the employment contract or existing policies or practices. For a foreign employee leaving employment, the employer must withhold monies due for tax clearance for up to 30 days after notifying the Comptroller of Income Tax; this can affect when salary is released. [MOM | Paying salary](https://www.mom.gov.sg/employment-practices/salary/paying-salary)

**Source:** MOM | Paying salary (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Final salary payment deadlines by termination reason): If you are covered by the Employment Act, your employer must pay your salary at least once a month.
They can also pay it at shorter intervals if they choose.
Salary must be paid:
Within 7 days after the end of the salary period.
For overtime work, within 14 days after the end of the salary period.

Your final salary payment could vary depending on the following situations:
In this situation | Your final salary must be paid
Employee resigns and serves the required notice period | On the last day of employment.
Employee resigns and does not serve the notice period | Within 7 days of the last day of employment.
Dismissal on grounds of misconduct | On the last day of employment. If this is not possible, then within 3 working days from date of dismissal.
Employer terminates the contract | On the last day of employment. If this is not possible, then within 3 working days from date of termination.

If your contract involves commission, how and when the commission is paid depends on what is in your employment contract or existing policies or practices.
If you’re a foreign employee who is leaving your employment, your employer is required to withhold all your monies due to you for tax clearance for up to 30 days upon giving notice of the cessation of your employment to the Comptroller of Income Tax. The monies include your salary, leave pay, etc.

outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.

#### Ministry of Manpower — Employment requirements

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Public holiday entitlement and pay** (party in scope: Employee)
- **MOM rule explanation:** An Employment Act-covered employee has 11 paid public holidays each year. If a holiday falls on the rest day, the following working day will be a paid public holiday; if it falls on a non-working day, another day off or an extra day at the gross rate is due. Working on a public holiday ordinarily earns holiday gross pay plus an additional day at the basic rate; overtime applies beyond normal hours. By mutual agreement, the day may be substituted. Part IV coverage limits which employees may use time off in lieu. Distinguish a holiday on a working day, non-working day, or rest day. For holiday gross pay, the employee must not be absent without consent or reasonable excuse on the working day immediately before or after the holiday; authorised leave on either day is permitted. No holiday pay is due when the holiday itself falls during approved unpaid leave. Additional basic-rate pay is the default for working on the holiday; substitute-holiday arrangements require mutual agreement. An employee outside Employment Act coverage is governed by the contract. Time off in lieu of hours worked is available only to employees not covered by Part IV under the stated arrangement. Rest-day pay and any excess-hours overtime are separate entitlements. A case-specific conclusion requires: Employment Act and Part IV coverage. Work schedule and whether the date is a working, non-working or rest day. Whether the employee worked, hours worked, agreed substitution/time-off arrangements, and relevant absence or unpaid-leave facts. Does not decide a specific date’s gazetted holiday status or compute holiday pay without schedule and wage facts. Does not replace separate rest-day, overtime or part-time rules. [MOM | Public holidays: entitlement and pay](https://www.mom.gov.sg/employment-practices/public-holidays-entitlement-and-pay)

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.

#### Monetary Authority of Singapore — Financial regulation

**Status:** Evidence verified

**MAS LFMC toolkit scope and fund-level requirements** (party in scope: Company)
- **MAS rule explanation:** The MAS LFMC toolkit is a reference for common SFA approvals, notifications and regulatory submissions applicable to LFMCs. MAS says it is not exhaustive and expressly excludes obligations outside the SFA and fund-level requirements, such as the Code of Collective Investment Schemes. It therefore is not a complete checklist for all duties affecting a managed fund. Identify applicable fund-level requirements and other legislation separately. This scope statement applies to the LFMC toolkit; it does not establish the scope of VCFM or other licence-class toolkits. [LICENSED FUND MANAGEMENT COMPANIES](https://www.mas.gov.sg/-/media/mas-media-library/regulation/guidance/cmi/compliance-toolkits-for-fund-management-companies/sfa-compliance-toolkit-lfmcs29-may-2026-clean.pdf)

- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports MAS LFMC toolkit scope and fund-level requirements): This compliance toolkit aims to provide LFMCs with a simple reference on the common applications, forms and submissions pursuant to the SFA that are applicable to LFMCs. However, it is not exhaustive, and LFMCs are expected to be familiar with all legislations and requirements that are applicable to them.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports MAS LFMC toolkit scope and fund-level requirements): For the avoidance of doubt, this toolkit excludes reporting obligations that fall outside the SFA; as well as fund-level requirements (e.g. Code of Collective Investment Scheme).

outcomes.question: Notice SFA 04-N24 says it takes effect on 1 January 2027. Does its 21-day reporting rule already settle what a CMS licence holder had to do for misconduct first suspected in December 2026?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for the issues identified below; other issues remain incomplete.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** See the evidence gaps and coverage limitations below.

**Applicability limitation:** The available evidence does not establish the requested rule for 2027. An official source whose legal applicability covers that period is needed. A current page, its retrieval date, or a document's original issue date alone cannot establish the requirements for an earlier or later period.

#### Monetary Authority of Singapore — Financial regulation

**Status:** Evidence incomplete

**Capital Markets Services Licence** (party in scope: Not established)
- **Evidence gap:** The issue has no resolved authority and topic mapping for this workstream.

**SFA 04-N24 reporting of misconduct by representatives from 1 January 2027** (party in scope: Company)
- **MAS rule explanation:** MAS Notice SFA 04-N24 takes effect on 1 January 2027. It applies to CMS licence holders and persons exempt under SFA section 99(1)(a)–(d), for misconduct by their representatives and former representatives. A CMI must submit a Misconduct Report no later than 21 calendar days after the date it first has reasonable grounds to believe the current or former representative committed misconduct during the representative period, unless the Authority allows a longer period in writing. Paragraph 21 keeps the cancelled Notice applicable where a report was submitted before 1 January 2027 or was required by 31 December 2026. Paragraph 20 addresses a pre-2027 reasonable-grounds case where no Misconduct Report in the form set out in the cancelled Notice had been submitted by 1 January 2027: the report under SFA 04-N24 is due within 21 calendar days after 1 January 2027, or a longer period allowed in writing. A case-specific conclusion requires the CMI status, representative period, reasonable-grounds date and transition facts. The ordinary SFA 04-N24 rule is not yet in effect for an October or December 2026 matter. The 2027 notice does not by itself establish what earlier reporting duty applied or prove that none existed. Paragraph 21 must be checked first: it continues the cancelled Notice for matters with a report already submitted before 1 January 2027 or due by 31 December 2026. Paragraph 20 applies only to its separate pre-2027 reasonable-grounds cases not covered by that paragraph 21 transition. [NOTICE ON REPORTING | OF MISCONDUCT OF](https://www.mas.gov.sg/-/media/mas-media-library/regulation/notices/cmg/notice-sfa-04-n24/notice-sfa-04-n24-reporting-of-misconduct-of-representatives.pdf?hash=C027656887BDCD18A5742523AA08B2A1&sc_lang=en)

sources.sourceText:
1 | This Notice (excluding the Annexes) is issued pursuant to section 101(1) of the Securities and Futures Act 2001 ("the Act") and takes effect from 1 January 2027. Notice No. SFA 04-N11 issued on 26 November 2010 is cancelled with effect from 1 January 2027.

2 This Notice shall apply to all holders of a capital markets services ("CMS") licence and persons who are exempt from holding a CMS licence under section 99(1)(a), (b), (c) or (d) of the Act. It sets out the reporting requirements for the misconduct of their representatives and former representatives.

5 | If a CMI has reasonable grounds to believe that — (a) its representative had committed any misconduct; or Notice on Reporting of Misconduct of Representatives by Holders of Capital Markets Services Licence and Exempt Persons 3 (b) its former representative had committed any misconduct during the period when he or she was a representative of the CMI, the CMI must submit a Misconduct Report to the Authority, providing all the applicable information required therein in relation to the misconduct (called in this Notice "alleged misconduct"), no later than 21 calendar days, or such longer period as the Authority may allow in writing, after the date on which the CMI first has reasonable grounds to believe that which is mentioned in sub-paragraph (a) or (b).

20 Despite paragraph 5, where a CMI — (a) first had reasonable grounds to believe, before 1 January 2027, that any type of misconduct within the definition of "misconduct" in paragraph 3 of this Notice was committed by its representative or its former representative when he or she was its representative; and (b) has not submitted to the Authority a Misconduct Report, which is in the form set out at Appendix 1 of the Notice on Reporting of Misconduct of Representatives by Holders of Capital Markets Services Licence and Exempt Financial Institutions (MAS Notice No. SFA 04-N11) (" Cancelled Notice "), in relation to the misconduct before 1 January 2027, the CMI must submit to the Authority a Misconduct Report in relation to the misconduct under this Notice and any other document or information that may be required under paragraphs 6 to 8 of this Notice, no later than 21 calendar days, or such longer period as the Authority may allow in writing, after 1 January 2027.

21 This Notice does not apply to or in relation to any of the following, and despite paragraph 1, the Cancelled Notice as in force immediately before 1 January 2027 continues to apply to or in relation to any of the following as if this Notice has not been issued: (a) any case for which a CMI submitted a Misconduct Report under the Cancelled Notice (which is in the form set out at Appendix 1 of that Notice) before 1 January 2027; (b) any case for which a CMI was required under the Cancelled Notice to submit a Misconduct Report (which is in the form set out at Appendix 1 of that Notice) by 31 December 2026, save that a reference in the Cancelled Notice to "MASNET" is to MASNET or any electronic system which may be established by the Authority in place of MASNET.
